note: A ship goes large when the wind blows from behind or a little to one side, so she sails easily.
source: W. H. Smyth, The Sailor’s Word-Book (1867), “Large”, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/26000

anchor: some sportful talk with the members of his mess
note: Sportful: playful. A mess is a group of sailors who eat together.
source: W. H. Smyth, The Sailor’s Word-Book (1867), “Mess”, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/26000

anchor: a sudden lurch to spill the entire contents of his soup-pan
note: Lurch: a sudden roll of the ship.
Sailors scrubbed the decks clean every day.
A rattan is a cane made from a palm stem, here the master-at-arms’ badge and tool of authority.

anchor: along the battery in a bay of which the mess was lodged
note: A battery is a row of guns on a deck; a bay is the space between two guns.

anchor: he was about to ejaculate something hasty
playfully tapped him from behind with his rattan
note: Claggart’s manner is playful on the surface but his words are loaded.

anchor: “Handsomely done, my lad! And handsome is as handsome did it too!”
note: The proverb says handsome is as handsome does. Claggart twists it to mock Billy’s looks.

anchor: the involuntary smile, or rather grimace
note: Grimace: a twisted face expressing pain or disgust.

anchor: Aridly it drew down the thin corners
note: Aridly: dryly, without warmth. His smile draws the corners of his mouth down.
Counterfeited: faked. Glee: laughter. They laugh at a superior’s joke because they must.
Donald is a Scottish messmate, later Billy’s friend.
Smoky: obscure and unclear, like the Dansker’s warnings.

anchor: usurping the face from the heart
note: Usurping: taking over by force. A hidden feeling seizes his face.
A drummer-boy beat signals on a warship. Heedlessly: carelessly.
